title: Measurement and Study Design
description: Choose measures and designs that answer research questions.

questions.prompt: Construct validity asks whether a measure:
options: Produces the same score every time only
questions.explanation: Construct validity concerns evidence that scores represent the intended construct for the proposed use.

questions.prompt: A measure can be reliable without being valid for the intended purpose.
questions.explanation: Consistency alone does not ensure the measure captures the target concept.

questions.prompt: Which may threaten measurement quality?
questions.explanation: Unclear items, response pressures, and faulty instruments can distort observations; preregistration improves transparency.

questions.prompt: Operationalizing a construct requires making the chosen measurement procedure explicit.
questions.explanation: Operational definitions clarify how an abstract concept is represented in a study.

questions.prompt: A sampling frame is:
options: The list or mechanism from which a sample is drawn
questions.explanation: The frame determines which units can be selected and may omit parts of the target population.

questions.prompt: A large sample automatically eliminates selection bias.
questions.explanation: Size can reduce random error but does not correct systematic selection or nonresponse.

questions.prompt: Which improve a survey item?
options: Ask one clear question at a time
Combine two topics in one item
questions.explanation: Single, balanced items with clear timeframes reduce ambiguity and response burden.

questions.prompt: Random sampling and random assignment serve different purposes.
questions.explanation: Sampling supports population representation; assignment supports group comparability in experiments.

questions.prompt: A longitudinal study is designed to:
questions.explanation: Repeated observations track change, though time trends and confounding complicate inference.

questions.prompt: A cross-sectional association alone establishes how an individual changes over time.
questions.explanation: Cross-sectional data capture a snapshot and cannot directly show within-person change.

questions.prompt: Which are useful design choices for a qualitative interview study?
questions.explanation: Open prompts, transparent sampling, and reflexivity support rigor; quotes are not population estimates.

questions.prompt: A pilot study can reveal confusing procedures before a larger study begins.
questions.explanation: Piloting assesses feasibility and comprehension but is not definitive evidence of effectiveness.

questions.prompt: A manipulation check assesses:
options: Whether the intended manipulation changed its target
questions.explanation: It tests whether the intervention altered the intended construct or condition.

questions.prompt: A failed manipulation check always means the theory is false.
questions.explanation: Failure may reflect implementation, measurement, or theoretical issues and needs diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a clear methods description?
questions.explanation: Transparent methods let readers assess bias and understand how results were produced.

questions.prompt: Blinding can reduce some expectancy effects in research.
questions.explanation: Masking condition knowledge can limit bias in participants, assessors, or analysts when feasible.

questions.prompt: A ceiling effect limits a measure because:
options: Many scores cluster near its maximum
questions.explanation: A task that is too easy cannot distinguish higher levels of the construct.

questions.prompt: Measurement invariance matters when comparing scores across groups.
questions.explanation: Researchers should examine whether a measure functions comparably before interpreting group differences.

questions.prompt: Which can improve response rates without compromising ethics?
questions.explanation: Low-burden, clear, accessible invitations support participation without coercion.

questions.prompt: Self-report is always inferior to behavioral measurement.
questions.explanation: Each approach has strengths and limitations; the best measure depends on the construct and question.
